blocks.content: When your program opens a file, sends a network request, or prints to the screen, it does not do any of that itself. It cannot. Those actions touch hardware, and a normal program is not allowed near the hardware. Instead, it asks the operating system to do the work on its behalf. The mechanism for asking is the system call.

A system call is the bridge between your program in user space and the kernel that controls the machine. Almost everything interesting a program does, files, networking, creating processes, eventually goes through a system call.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308463-627609541.png
1. What a System Call Is

A system call is a request from a program to the operating system kernel to perform an action that the program is not allowed to do by itself. It is the controlled way for user space code to reach the privileged services of the kernel.

Reading a file, writing to the network, allocating memory, and starting a new process are all privileged operations. A program cannot perform them directly, so it makes a system call, and the kernel carries out the request safely.

["A request from a program to the kernel for a privileged action","The only sanctioned way for user code to reach kernel services","Used for files, networking, memory, processes, and more","The kernel checks each request before performing it"]
items: A request from a program to the kernel for a privileged action
The only sanctioned way for user code to reach kernel services
Used for files, networking, memory, processes, and more
The kernel checks each request before performing it

blocks.title: A simple picture
blocks.content: A system call is like ordering at a restaurant. You do not walk into the kitchen and cook, you hand your order to a waiter, who takes it to the kitchen and brings the result back. The kitchen, the kernel, stays protected.
2. Why System Calls Exist

System calls exist because of the wall between user space and kernel space. Programs run in a restricted user mode where privileged instructions are forbidden, precisely so a buggy or malicious program cannot damage the system.

But programs still need to do useful, privileged things. The system call is the carefully guarded gate in that wall. It lets a program request a privileged action without ever being given privileged power itself.

["User programs run restricted and cannot touch hardware directly","They still need privileged actions like reading files","The system call is the controlled gate through the wall","It gives access to a service without giving the program raw power"]
items: User programs run restricted and cannot touch hardware directly
They still need privileged actions like reading files
The system call is the controlled gate through the wall
It gives access to a service without giving the program raw power

blocks.title: Access without power
blocks.content: The genius of the system call is that a program gains the ability to do privileged things while never holding privileged power itself. It only ever asks, and the kernel decides.
3. How a System Call Works
Under the hood, a system call is more than a normal function call, because it has to switch the processor from restricted user mode into privileged kernel mode and back.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308463-544685275.png

["The program puts the system call number and its arguments into CPU registers","It runs a special trap instruction that switches the CPU into kernel mode","The kernel looks up the call number and runs the matching handler","The kernel performs the work, checking that it is allowed","Control returns to the program in user mode, with the result"]
items: The program puts the system call number and its arguments into CPU registers
It runs a special trap instruction that switches the CPU into kernel mode
The kernel looks up the call number and runs the matching handler
The kernel performs the work, checking that it is allowed
Control returns to the program in user mode, with the result

blocks.content: The trap instruction is the key. A normal jump cannot change the privilege level, but the trap safely enters the kernel at a fixed, controlled point. This is why a program cannot sneak into arbitrary kernel code, it can only enter through the front door the kernel provides.
4. The Anatomy of a Call
Every system call is identified by a number. The operating system keeps a table, the system call table, that maps each number to the kernel function that handles it.

When a program makes a call, it places that number in a register along with the arguments, then traps into the kernel. The kernel reads the number, finds the right function in the table, and runs it. This is why system calls are referred to both by name, like read, and by their number underneath.

["Each system call has a unique number","The system call table maps numbers to kernel handler functions","Arguments are passed in registers alongside the number","The kernel validates the arguments before acting on them"]
items: Each system call has a unique number
The system call table maps numbers to kernel handler functions
Arguments are passed in registers alongside the number
The kernel validates the arguments before acting on them

blocks.title: Numbers under the names
blocks.content: You write read or open, but underneath each is just a number the kernel looks up in its table. The friendly name is provided by a library wrapper around the raw numbered call.
5. Categories of System Calls
There are many system calls, but they group into a handful of categories based on what they manage.

{"headers":["Category","What it does","Examples"],"rows":[["Process control","Create, run, and end processes","fork, exec, exit, wait"],["File management","Work with files","open, read, write, close"],["Device management","Talk to devices","ioctl, read, write"],["Information","Get or set system data","getpid, time, uname"],["Communication","Move data between processes","pipe, socket, send"],["Protection","Control access and permissions","chmod, umask"]]}

You rarely need to memorise the full list. What matters is recognising that every category is about crossing into the kernel to manage a resource the program cannot touch on its own, whether that is a process, a file, a device, or another process.
6. Common System Calls
A few system calls appear constantly, and seeing them makes the idea concrete.

int fd = open("data.txt", O_RDONLY);  // ask the kernel to open a file
read(fd, buffer, 100);                 // ask the kernel to read 100 bytes
write(1, "hello", 5);                  // ask the kernel to write to the screen
close(fd);                             // ask the kernel to close the file
blocks.code:

read(fd, buffer, 100);                 // ask the kernel to read 100 bytes
write(1, "hello", 5);                  // ask the kernel to write to the screen
close(fd);                             // ask the kernel to close the file

int fd = open("data.txt", O_RDONLY);  // ask the kernel to open a file
read(fd, buffer, 100);                 // ask the kernel to read 100 bytes
write(1, "hello", 5);                  // ask the kernel to write to the screen
close(fd);                             // ask the kernel to close the file

blocks.content: Process related calls are just as important. The fork call creates a new process by duplicating the current one, and exec replaces a process with a new program. Together they are how one program launches another, which is the foundation of how a shell runs commands.
["open, read, write, close for working with files","fork and exec for creating and running programs","socket, send, recv for networking","exit and wait for ending and coordinating processes"]
items: open, read, write, close for working with files
fork and exec for creating and running programs
socket, send, recv for networking
exit and wait for ending and coordinating processes

blocks.content: 7. System Calls vs Library Functions
A common confusion is the difference between a system call and an ordinary library function, because they look the same in your code.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308463-158483149.png

A library function runs entirely in user space. A system call crosses into the kernel. Often a library function is a friendly wrapper that eventually makes a system call. When you call printf, it formats your text in user space, then calls the write system call to actually put the bytes on the screen.

["A library function runs in user space, with no kernel crossing","A system call crosses into the kernel for a privileged action","Many library functions wrap a system call underneath","printf formats text, then uses the write system call to output it"]
items: A library function runs in user space, with no kernel crossing
A system call crosses into the kernel for a privileged action
Many library functions wrap a system call underneath
printf formats text, then uses the write system call to output it

blocks.title: Not every call is a system call
blocks.content: Doing math or formatting a string never needs the kernel, so those stay in user space and are cheap. Only the calls that touch a resource outside the program become system calls.
8. The Cost of a System Call
blocks.text: 8. The Cost of a System Call

blocks.content: Because a system call switches the CPU between user mode and kernel mode, it costs more than an ordinary function call. The processor has to change privilege levels and save and restore some state each time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408308464-793674041.png
blocks.alt: The Cost of a System Call

blocks.content: A single system call is fast, but the cost adds up if you make a huge number of them. This is why efficient programs try to do more work per call, for example by reading and writing in large chunks rather than one byte at a time.

["A system call is more expensive than a normal function call","The cost comes from switching privilege modes and saving state","One call is cheap, but millions of calls are not","Programs batch work, like buffering input and output, to make fewer calls"]
items: A system call is more expensive than a normal function call
The cost comes from switching privilege modes and saving state
One call is cheap, but millions of calls are not
Programs batch work, like buffering input and output, to make fewer calls

blocks.content: 9. Seeing System Calls in Action
System calls are not just theory, you can watch a program make them. On Linux the tool strace prints every system call a program makes, and on macOS the equivalent is dtruss.

Running a simple command under strace is eye opening. Even printing hello world triggers a series of system calls to load the program, open the output, write the text, and exit. It makes visible just how often programs lean on the kernel.

["strace on Linux shows every system call a program makes","Even a tiny program makes many calls to load, run, and exit","It is a great way to understand and debug what a program is really doing","Seeing the calls makes the user and kernel boundary feel concrete"]
items: strace on Linux shows every system call a program makes
Even a tiny program makes many calls to load, run, and exit
It is a great way to understand and debug what a program is really doing
Seeing the calls makes the user and kernel boundary feel concrete

blocks.title: Watch a program talk to the kernel
blocks.content: Running a command under strace turns the abstract idea of system calls into a live list you can read. It is one of the best ways to build real intuition for how programs and the kernel interact.
10. Key Takeaways

It is the only controlled way for user code to reach kernel services
